| showTableau(tree) | The tree as text. |

| foEntails(premises, conclusion, { maxSize, budget }) | Tree, then countermodel search, then a longer tree. |

### Try it

```js
// "There is a barber who shaves exactly those who do not shave themselves."
// Start a tree from that sentence alone (no conclusion): every branch closes,
// so it cannot be true in any structure, and no such barber exists.
const barber = "∃x ∀y (S(x, y) ↔ ¬S(y, y))";
const r = foTableau(barber);
PRINT("every branch closes:", r.status === "valid");
PRINT(showTableau(r.tree));

// And the classic quantifier swap, in the right direction
foEntails("∃y ∀x L(x, y)", "∀x ∃y L(x, y)").status
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/logic/circuits.html

Topic

## Circuits and Karnaugh maps

A circuit is a formula with its parts shared: gates wired together, with no loops. Two numbers describe its cost, the number of gates (size) and the longest path from an input to an output (depth, roughly the time a signal takes).

### Building and running a circuit

Gates are named, and each lists its kind and what it reads. The kinds are `and`, `or`, `xor`, `nand`, `nor`, `xnor` (two inputs or more), `not` and `buf`. A wiring that loops is refused.

```js
import { circuit } from "@ratmath/logic";

const half = circuit({ inputs: ["a", "b"],
  gates: { s: ["xor", "a", "b"], c: ["and", "a", "b"] }, outputs: ["s", "c"] });
half.evaluate([1, 1]);           // { s: 0, c: 1 }
half.size, half.depth;           // 2, 1
String(half.formula("s"));       // "a ⊕ b"
half.truthTable()[3];            // { inputs: [1, 1], outputs: { s: 0, c: 1 } }
```

### Adders

A full adder adds three bits: sum=a⊕b⊕cin​ and cout​=(a∧b)∨((a⊕b)∧cin​). Chaining n of them, each carry feeding the next, gives a ripple-carry adder for n-bit numbers. Its depth grows with n, because the last carry waits for all the others; faster adders look ahead at the carries.

```js
import { adders } from "@ratmath/logic";

const fa = adders.full();
fa.size, fa.depth, fa.counts;    // 5, 3, { xor: 2, and: 2, or: 1 }

const r4 = adders.ripple(4);     // inputs a3 a2 a1 a0 b3 b2 b1 b0, outputs c3 s3 s2 s1 s0
r4.evaluate([0,1,1,1, 0,1,0,1]); // { c3: 0, s3: 1, s2: 1, s1: 0, s0: 0 }: 7 + 5 = 12
r4.size, r4.depth;               // 17, 7
```

The tests check the 4-bit adder on all 256 pairs of inputs against ordinary addition.

### One kind of gate is enough

NAND alone can build everything: ¬a=a↑a, a∧b=¬(a↑b), and a∨b=¬a↑¬b. NOR is the same with the roles of and and or swapped. `circuitFrom` builds a circuit for a formula in standard gates, or in one of these, sharing equal parts and cancelling double negations.

```js
import { circuitFrom, circuitsEquivalent } from "@ratmath/logic";

const n = circuitFrom("(a & b) | ~c", { gates: "nand" });
n.counts;                        // { nand: 2 }: (a ↑ b) ↑ c
circuitsEquivalent(n, "(a & b) | ~c");   // { status: "equivalent" }
circuitsEquivalent(n, "(a & b) | c");
// { status: "different", output: "out", inputs: { a: 1, b: 0, c: 0 }, values: [1, 0] }
```

Equivalence is decided by the [solver](https://ratmath.com/logic/satisfiability.html), and a difference comes with an input where the two disagree, checked by running both.

### Karnaugh maps

A Karnaugh map lays out a truth table of up to four atoms as a grid whose rows and columns are in Gray code order (00, 01, 11, 10), so neighbouring cells, including across the edges, differ in one atom. A block of 1, 2, 4 or 8 true cells in a rectangle is then a single product term: the atoms that stay the same across the block. Covering every 1 with as few, as large, blocks as possible gives a shortest sum of products.

```js
import { karnaugh } from "@ratmath/logic";

const k = karnaugh("(a & b) | (~a & c) | (b & c) | (d & ~b & a)");
k.toString();
// ab\cd   00  01  11  10
// 00       0   0   1   1
// 01       0   0   1   1
// 11       1   1   1   1
// 10       0   1   1   0
k.groups.map((g) => String(g.formula));   // ["a ∧ b", "a ∧ d", "¬a ∧ c"], each a block of 4
String(k.formula);                         // "(a ∧ b) ∨ (a ∧ d) ∨ (¬a ∧ c)"

String(karnaugh({ minterms: [0, 2, 8, 10], atoms: ["a", "b", "c", "d"] }).formula);
// "¬b ∧ ¬d": the four corners are one block, because the edges wrap
```

Cells marked `x` are rows that do not matter (a `dontCares` list); a block may use them or not. The blocks are chosen by the same Quine–McCluskey method as [Simplification](https://ratmath.com/logic/simplification.html), so the map and the minimiser always agree.

```js
karnaugh({ minterms: [1, 3, 7], dontCares: [5], atoms: ["a", "b", "c"] }).formula;   // c
```

### Reference

| Export | What it does |

| circuit({ inputs, gates, outputs }) | A Circuit: evaluate(values), truthTable(), formula(output), size, depth, counts. |

| circuitFrom(f, { gates, output }) | gates: "standard", "nand" or "nor". |

| circuitsEquivalent(a, b) | Circuits or formulas, outputs matched by position. "equivalent", or "different" with the inputs that show it. |

| adders.half(), adders.full(), adders.ripple(n) | Adders built from gates. |

| karnaugh(f \| { minterms, atoms, dontCares }) | Two to four atoms. cells, rowLabels, colLabels, groups (each with formula, cells, size, essential), formula, toString(). |

### Try it

```js
// A majority vote of three: true when at least two inputs are.
const maj = "(a & b) | (a & c) | (b & c)";
const k = karnaugh(maj);
PRINT(k.toString());
PRINT("groups:", k.groups.map((g) => String(g.formula)).join(", "));

// In NAND gates only, then checked against the formula
const n = circuitFrom(maj, { gates: "nand" });
PRINT("NAND gates:", n.counts.nand, " depth:", n.depth);
PRINT(circuitsEquivalent(n, maj).status);

// A two-bit ripple adder: 3 + 2
adders.ripple(2).evaluate([1, 1, 1, 0])
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/logic/syllogisms.html

Topic

## Syllogisms

For two thousand years logic meant the syllogism: two premises and a conclusion, each saying how two classes are related. Here validity is not looked up in a list. It is decided, by checking every way of filling in a Venn diagram, and the traditional names and rules are reported beside the answer.

### Four forms of statement

| Form | Statement | On the Venn diagram |

| A | All S are P | S outside P is empty |

| E | No S are P | S inside P is empty |

| I | Some S are P | S inside P has something in it |

| O | Some S are not P | S outside P has something in it |

```js
import { categorical, categoricalText } from "@ratmath/logic";

categorical("No reptiles are mammals");     // { form: "E", subject: "reptiles", predicate: "mammals" }
categoricalText({ form: "O", subject: "birds", predicate: "fliers" });   // "Some birds are not fliers"
```

### Mood and figure

A syllogism has three terms: the minor term S (the subject of the conclusion), the major term P (its predicate), and the middle term M, which appears in both premises and not in the conclusion. The major premise, written first, contains P. The mood is the three forms in order, and the figure (1 to 4) says where M stands:

| Figure | Major premise | Minor premise |

| 1 | M – P | S – M |

| 2 | P – M | S – M |

| 3 | M – P | M – S |

| 4 | P – M | M – S |

So there are 43×4=256 syllogisms. Give one in words, or by mood and figure:

```js
import { syllogism } from "@ratmath/logic";

const s = syllogism("All men are mortal", "All Greeks are men", "All Greeks are mortal");
s.valid, s.form, s.name;    // true, "AAA-1", "Barbara"
s.terms;                    // { S: "Greeks", M: "men", P: "mortal" }
s.venn.shaded;              // ["¬SM¬P", "S¬M¬P", "S¬MP", "SM¬P"]: the regions forced empty

syllogism("EIO-2", { S: "poets", M: "rich", P: "happy" }).statements;
// ["No happy are rich", "Some poets are rich", "Some poets are not happy"]
```

### Deciding validity

The three circles of a Venn diagram make eight regions. A statement says some regions are empty, or that some region among a few has something in it. Each of the 28=256 choices of which regions have something in them either makes the premises true or not; the syllogism is valid when every choice that makes the premises true makes the conclusion true. If one does not, it is a counterexample, and the fewest occupied regions are reported.

```js
const bad = syllogism("All dogs are animals", "All cats are animals", "All cats are dogs");
bad.valid;               // false
bad.counterexample;      // ["SM¬P"]: a cat that is an animal and not a dog
bad.rules.filter((r) => r.broken).map((r) => r.rule);
// ["the middle term is distributed at least once"]
```

The tests build actual sets from each counterexample, one element per occupied region, and check that the premises come out true and the conclusion false, for every invalid syllogism.

### Existential import

Aristotle took every term to have members, so "All S are P" carried "Some S are P" with it. Modern logic does not: "All unicorns have horns" is true because there are no unicorns. The modern reading has 15 valid syllogisms; with existential import, nine more become valid, each with its own name.

```js
syllogism("AAI-3").valid;              // false: "All M are P, All M are S, so Some S are P"
syllogism("AAI-3").counterexample;     // []: everything empty
syllogism("AAI-3", { existentialImport: true }).name;   // "Darapti"

validSyllogisms().map((x) => x.name).join(", ");
// "Barbara, Camestres, Calemes, Darii, Datisi, Baroco, Celarent, Cesare,
//  Ferio, Festino, Ferison, Fresison, Disamis, Dimatis, Bocardo"
```

### The traditional rules

Medieval logicians gave rules that a valid syllogism keeps. A term is distributed when the statement says something about all of it: the subject of A and E, the predicate of E and O.

- The middle term is distributed at least once.

- A term distributed in the conclusion is distributed in its premise (otherwise "illicit major" or "illicit minor").

- Not both premises are negative.

- A negative premise needs a negative conclusion, and a negative conclusion needs a negative premise.

- On the modern reading, two universal premises do not give a particular conclusion.

Each result lists the rules and which are broken. A syllogism is valid exactly when it breaks none, which the tests check against the Venn decision on all 256.

### Reference

| Export | What it does |

| categorical(text \| { form, subject, predicate }) | A statement in one of the four forms. |

| categoricalText(statement) | The statement in words. |

| syllogism(major, minor, conclusion, { existentialImport }) | Decide a syllogism given in words or as objects. |

| syllogism("AAA-1", { existentialImport, S, M, P }) | Decide by mood and figure, with names for the terms if you like. |

| result | valid, mood, figure, form, name, terms, statements, counterexample (occupied regions), venn (shaded, marked), rules. |

| validSyllogisms({ existentialImport }) | Every valid mood and figure with its name: 15, or 24 with existential import. |

### Try it

```js
// Is this valid? If so, what is it called; if not, which rule does it break?
const r = syllogism("No heroes are cowards", "Some soldiers are cowards", "Some soldiers are not heroes");
PRINT(r.form, r.valid ? "valid: " + r.name : "invalid");
PRINT("statements:", r.statements.join(" / "));
PRINT("broken rules:", r.rules.filter((x) => x.broken).map((x) => x.rule).join("; ") || "none");

// Every mood that becomes valid only with existential import
const modern = new Set(validSyllogisms().map((x) => x.form));
validSyllogisms({ existentialImport: true }).filter((x) => !modern.has(x.form)).map((x) => `${x.form} ${x.name}`)
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/logic/modal-logic.html

Topic

## Modal logic

Modal logic adds two operators: □A, "necessarily A", and ◊A, "possibly A". Read them as knowledge, obligation, provability or time, and the same machinery applies. What changes from reading to reading is which axioms hold, and Kripke's semantics ties each axiom to a property of a picture.

### Formulas

Write □ as `□`, `[]`, `box` or `nec`, and ◊ as `◇`, `<>`, `dia` or `poss`. Everything else is propositional. ◊A means the same as ¬□¬A.

```js
import { parseModal } from "@ratmath/logic";

const f = parseModal("[]p -> <>p");
String(f);                        // "□p → ◇p"
f.modalDepth;                     // 1
String(parseModal("box p -> dia p"));   // "□p → ◇p"
```

### Kripke models

A Kripke model is a set of worlds, an accessibility relation saying which worlds each world "sees", and a valuation saying where each atom is true. Then □A is true at w when A is true at every world w sees, and ◊A when A is true at some world w sees. A world that sees nothing makes every □A true, even □⊥.

```js
import { kripke } from "@ratmath/logic";

const M = kripke({ worlds: ["a", "b", "c"],
  access: [["a", "b"], ["a", "c"], ["b", "b"]], valuation: { p: ["b"] } });
M.truthAt("◇p ∧ ◇¬p", "a");      // true: a sees b (p) and c (not p)
M.truthAt("□⊥", "c");            // true: c sees nothing
M.trueAt("□p");                  // ["b", "c"]
M.truthAt("□p", "a", { explain: true }).steps[0];
// "□p at a: false (p fails at c, which a sees)"
```

### Axioms and frames

A frame is a Kripke model without the valuation. A formula is valid on a frame when it is true at every world under every valuation, and some formulas are valid exactly on the frames with a property:

| Axiom | Formula | Valid exactly on frames that are |

| K | □(p→q)→(□p→□q) | all frames |

| D | □p→◊p | serial: every world sees some world |

| T | □p→p | reflexive |

| B | p→□◊p | symmetric |

| 4 | □p→□□p | transitive |

| 5 | ◊p→□◊p | euclidean |

The usual systems are named for their frames: K (any), D (serial), T (reflexive), B (reflexive and symmetric), S4 (reflexive and transitive) and S5 (all three, an equivalence relation). For knowledge, T says that what is known is true; 4 says that what is known is known to be known.

```js
import { validOnFrame, SYSTEMS } from "@ratmath/logic";

validOnFrame("□p → p", { worlds: 2, access: [["w1", "w1"], ["w2", "w2"], ["w1", "w2"]] });
// { valid: true }: the frame is reflexive
const v = validOnFrame("□p → □□p", { worlds: 3, access: [["w1", "w2"], ["w2", "w3"]] });
v.valid, v.valuation, v.world;    // false, { p: ["w2"] }, "w1": the frame is not transitive
```

### Deciding validity

`modalValid` builds a truth tree with each formula labelled by its world. ¬□A at w creates a new world that w sees, with ¬A there; □A at w sends A to every world w sees. The frame properties of the system add edges: a loop at each world for T, an edge back for B, edges through for S4. If every branch closes, the formula is valid in the system. If a branch stays open, its worlds and edges are a countermodel, which is checked to be a frame of the system and to make the formula false.

```js
import { modalValid, showModalTree } from "@ratmath/logic";

modalValid("□p → p").status;                   // "invalid" in K
modalValid("□p → p").countermodel.describe();
// { worlds: ["w1"], access: { w1: [] }, valuation: { p: [] } }
modalValid("□p → p", { system: "T" }).status;  // "valid"

const r = modalValid("◇p → □◇p", { system: "S4" });
r.status;                                      // "invalid": axiom 5 needs S5
r.countermodel.describe().access;              // { w1: ["w2", "w3", "w1"], w2: ["w2"], w3: ["w3"] }

showModalTree(modalValid("□(p→q)→(□p→□q)").tree);
// w1: ¬(□(p → q) → (□p → □q))    (the formula is assumed false at w1)
// w1: □(p → q)    …
// w2: w1 sees w2    (for ¬□q at w1)
// w2: ¬q    (from ¬□q at w1)
// …
//   × closed: q and ¬q at w2
```

In S4 and S5 a tree could keep making worlds forever. A world whose formulas already appear at an earlier world is given no new successors; it points back to that world instead, which keeps every tree finite. The tests check the whole table of axioms against all six systems, and every countermodel against its frame conditions.

### Reference

| Export | What it does |

| parseModal(text), modal(x) | A ModalFormula: atoms(), modalDepth, toString({ style }). |

| kripke({ worlds, access, valuation }) | A Kripke model: sees(w), truthAt(f, w, { explain }), trueAt(f), holds(f), properties(), describe(). |

| SYSTEMS | The frame conditions of K, D, T, B, S4 and S5. |

| validOnFrame(f, frame) | Every valuation tried (up to 220); { valid }, or a valuation and world where it fails. |

| modalValid(f, { system, budget }) | "valid" with the closed tree, "invalid" with a checked countermodel, or "unresolved". |

| showModalTree(tree) | The tree as text. |

### Try it

```js
// Which systems prove which axioms? Each "-" comes with a countermodel.
const axioms = [["K", "□(p→q)→(□p→□q)"], ["D", "□p→◇p"], ["T", "□p→p"], ["B", "p→□◇p"], ["4", "□p→□□p"], ["5", "◇p→□◇p"]];
const systems = ["K", "D", "T", "B", "S4", "S5"];
PRINT("axiom  " + systems.map((s) => s.padEnd(3)).join(""));
for (const [name, f] of axioms) {
  PRINT(name.padEnd(7) + systems.map((s) => (modalValid(f, { system: s }).status === "valid" ? "✓" : "-").padEnd(3)).join(""));
}

// The countermodel to 4 in T
modalValid("□p→□□p", { system: "T" }).countermodel.describe()
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/logic/automata.html

Topic

## Automata and regular expressions

A finite automaton reads a word one symbol at a time, moving between finitely many states, and accepts or rejects at the end. The languages it can recognise are exactly those a regular expression can describe, and almost every question about them can be decided.

### Automata and runs

A DFA has one move for each state and symbol. An NFA may have several, or none, or moves on the empty word ε; it accepts when some way of running ends in an accepting state. Give the moves as a table:

```js
import { automaton } from "@ratmath/logic";

// words with an even number of a's
const even = automaton({ states: ["e", "o"], alphabet: "ab", start: "e", accept: ["e"],
  delta: { e: { a: "o", b: "e" }, o: { a: "e", b: "o" } } });
even.accepts("abba");     // true
even.run("aba").trace;    // [{ read: null, states: ["e"] }, { read: "a", states: ["o"] },
                          //  { read: "b", states: ["o"] }, { read: "a", states: ["e"] }]
even.words(3);            // ["", "b", "aa", "bb", "aab", "aba", "baa", "bbb"]
```

### From NFA to DFA, and the smallest DFA

An NFA is in a set of states at each step, so a DFA whose states are those sets does the same job (the subset construction). It can need 2n states for an n-state NFA, but usually far fewer are reachable. Then the DFA can be shrunk: two states that accept exactly the same continuations can be merged, and refining "accepting or not" until nothing splits gives the smallest DFA for the language, which is unique up to the names of its states (Myhill and Nerode).

```js
import { regexToNFA, toDFA, minimizeAutomaton } from "@ratmath/logic";

const n = regexToNFA("(a|b)*abb");     // 20 states, with ε moves
toDFA(n).states.length;                // 5
const m = minimizeAutomaton(n);
m.toString();
// start q0; accept q3
// q0 --a--> q1      q0 --b--> q0
// q1 --a--> q1      q1 --b--> q2
// q2 --a--> q1      q2 --b--> q3
// q3 --a--> q1      q3 --b--> q0
```

State qk​ remembers how much of `abb` the word has just read.

### Equivalence, with a reason

Two automata accept the same language exactly when, running both side by side, no reachable pair of states has one accepting and the other not. A breadth-first search over the pairs finds a shortest word that tells them apart, and the word is checked on both.

```js
import { equivalentAutomata } from "@ratmath/logic";

equivalentAutomata("(a|b)*", "(a*b*)*");   // { equivalent: true }
equivalentAutomata("a*b*", "(a|b)*");
// { equivalent: false, word: "ba", acceptedBy: "second" }
```

### Regular expressions

A regular expression is built from symbols, ε, union `|`, concatenation and star `*` (and `+`, `?` as shorthand). Thompson's construction turns each piece into a small NFA with one start and one end and joins them with ε moves. Going back, state elimination removes the states of an automaton one at a time, labelling the edges with ever larger expressions, until one edge from start to end is left (Kleene's theorem, both directions).

```js
import { toRegex } from "@ratmath/logic";

toRegex(even);    // "b*|b*a((b|ab*a)*)ab*"
```

The expressions that come back are correct but rarely the shortest; the tests check each against JavaScript's own regular expressions on every word up to length 7.

### Complements and products

Complete a DFA with a dead state and swap accepting and rejecting states, and it accepts the complement. Run two DFAs side by side, and accepting when both do (or either, or the first and not the second) gives intersection, union and difference. Regular languages are closed under all of these.

```js
import { complement, product } from "@ratmath/logic";

product(even, n, "and").words(5);   // ["aabb", "ababb", "baabb"]
complement(even).words(3);          // ["a", "ab", "ba", "aaa", "abb", "bab", "bba"]
```

### Reference

| Export | What it does |

| automaton({ states, alphabet, start, accept, delta }) | An Automaton: run(word) with a trace, accepts, words(maxLength), isDFA, isComplete, toString(). |

| toDFA(a), complete(a, alphabet) | The subset construction; every move defined, with a dead state ∅. |

| minimizeAutomaton(a) | The smallest DFA, with states named q0, q1, … |

| equivalentAutomata(a, b) | Automata or regular expressions. { equivalent }, with a shortest word when not. |

| complement(a, alphabet), product(a, b, op) | op: "and", "or" or "minus". |

| parseRegex(text), regexToNFA(regex), toRegex(a) | Regular expressions to automata (Thompson) and back (state elimination). |

### Try it

```js
// Binary numbers divisible by 3: the state is the remainder so far.
const div3 = automaton({ states: ["0", "1", "2"], alphabet: "01", start: "0", accept: ["0"],
  delta: { 0: { 0: "0", 1: "1" }, 1: { 0: "2", 1: "0" }, 2: { 0: "1", 1: "2" } } });
const numbers = div3.words(5).filter((w) => w === "0" || w[0] === "1");   // no leading zeros
PRINT("accepted up to length 5:", numbers.map((w) => `${w} = ${parseInt(w, 2)}`).join(", "));

// A regular expression for the same language, found by state elimination
const re = toRegex(div3);
PRINT("as a regex:", re);
PRINT("same language:", equivalentAutomata(re, div3).equivalent);

// Already minimal?
minimizeAutomaton(div3).states.length
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/logic/machines.html

Topic

## Grammars and machines

Beyond finite automata the machines get memory: a stack, then an unbounded tape. Each step up recognises more languages, and at the top, with Turing machines and recursive functions, the questions stop being decidable. Machines here run with a step budget, and a machine that has not halted is reported as running, never as rejecting.

### Context-free grammars

A grammar has rules that rewrite a nonterminal (a capital letter) into a string of symbols. The words it generates are the strings of terminals reachable from the start symbol. S→aSb∣ε generates anbn, which no finite automaton can recognise, since it would need to count without limit.

```js
import { grammar, showTree } from "@ratmath/logic";

const g = grammar("S -> a S b | ε");
g.words(8).words;        // ["", "ab", "aabb", "aaabbb", "aaaabbbb"]
showTree(g.parse("aabb").tree);   // "S(a S(a S(ε) b) b)"
```

Membership is decided by the CYK method. The grammar is first put in Chomsky normal form, where every rule is A→BC or A→a: ε-rules and unit rules are removed, and long rules are split. Then a table records which nonterminals generate each piece of the word, shortest pieces first, in time O(n3). When the word is accepted, a parse tree in the grammar as you wrote it is found too.

```js
g.toCNF().toString();
// S → T0 X0 | T0 T1
// X0 → S T1
// S0 → ε | T0 X0 | T0 T1
// T0 → a
// T1 → b

const e = grammar("E -> E + T | T\nT -> T * F | F\nF -> ( E ) | x");
showTree(e.parse("x+x*x").tree);   // "E(E(T(F(x))) + T(T(F(x)) * F(x)))": * binds tighter
e.accepts("x+*x");                  // false
```

### Pushdown automata

A pushdown automaton is a finite automaton with a stack. Each move reads a symbol (or nothing), pops the top of the stack (or nothing), and pushes a string. It accepts by ending in an accepting state. These machines recognise exactly the context-free languages. The run searches the possible computations breadth first and returns the accepting one it finds:

```js
import { pda } from "@ratmath/logic";

// a's push A, then each b pops one; accept when only Z is left
const anbn = pda({ start: "q0", accept: ["q2"], moves: [
  ["q0", "a", "ε", "q0", "A"], ["q0", "ε", "ε", "q1", "ε"],
  ["q1", "b", "A", "q1", "ε"], ["q1", "ε", "Z", "q2", "Z"]] });
anbn.run("aabb").trace.map((c) => `${c.state} ${c.read || "-"} ${c.stack}`);
// ["q0 - Z", "q0 a AZ", "q0 aa AAZ", "q1 aa AAZ", "q1 aab AZ", "q1 aabb Z", "q2 aabb Z"]
anbn.accepts("aab");    // false
```

### Turing machines

A Turing machine has a tape, unbounded both ways, and a head that reads a symbol, writes one, and moves left or right, according to a table indexed by state and symbol. Every algorithm can be written as one (the Church–Turing thesis), and so whether a machine halts cannot in general be decided: the halting problem. So `run` takes a budget, and a machine still going at the end is `"running"`.

```js
import { turing, binaryIncrement } from "@ratmath/logic";

binaryIncrement().run("1011", { trace: true });
// { status: "accepted", steps: 8, tape: "1100", trace: ["right: [1]011", "right: 1[0]11", …,
//   "carry: 101[1]_", "carry: 10[1]0_", "carry: 1[0]00_", "done: 1[1]00_"] }

turing({ start: "q", delta: { "q,_": ["q", "_", "R"] } }).run("", { budget: 50 }).status;
// "running": this one walks right forever, but the run only knows it has not stopped
```

A transition is written `"state,symbol": [new state, symbol written, move]`, with moves `L`, `R` or `S` (stay). With no transition the machine halts without accepting.

### Recursive functions

The other road to computability builds functions on the natural numbers from a few pieces: zero, successor, projections Pin​, composition, and primitive recursion: f(0,y​)=g(y​) and f(x+1,y​)=h(x,f(x,y​),y​). These are the primitive recursive functions, and every one of them halts. Adding minimisation, μx.f(x,y​)=0, the least zero, gives the general recursive functions, exactly the functions Turing machines compute, and with it the possibility of searching forever.

```js
import { recursive } from "@ratmath/logic";

const { add, mult, power, factorial } = recursive.examples;   // built only from the pieces
add.at(3, 4);            // 7n
power.at(2, 10);         // 1024n
factorial.at(7);         // 5040n

const { compose, proj } = recursive;
const double = compose(add, [proj(1, 1), proj(1, 1)]);
double.at(21);           // 42n
double.name;             // "add∘(P1^1,P1^1)"
```

These are computed the honest way, so addition takes x successor steps and multiplication repeats addition: keep the numbers small. `mu` stops at its budget and says that the search may never end.

### Reference

| Export | What it does |

| grammar(text \| { start, rules }) | A Grammar: words(maxLength), toCNF(), parse(word) (accepted, tree, cnfTree), accepts, toString(). |

| showTree(tree) | A parse tree as S(a S(…) b). |

| pda({ start, accept, stackStart, moves }) | A PDA; run(word, { budget }) gives "accepted" with a trace, "rejected", or "unresolved". |

| turing({ start, accept, reject, blank, delta }) | A TuringMachine; run(input, { budget, trace }) gives status ("accepted", "rejected", "halted", "running"), steps, tape, head. |

| binaryIncrement() | A machine that adds one to a binary number. |

| recursive | zero, succ, proj(i, n), compose(f, gs), primrec(g, h), mu(f, { budget }), constant(c, n), and examples: add, mult, pred, monus, power, factorial. Each has arity, name, at(...) on BigInt. |

### Try it

```js
// A Turing machine that checks a word of a's and b's is a palindrome:
// cross off the first symbol, run to the end, check it matches, come back.
const pal = turing({ start: "s", accept: "yes", reject: "no", delta: {
  "s,a": ["ra", "_", "R"], "s,b": ["rb", "_", "R"], "s,_": ["yes", "_", "S"],
  "ra,a": ["ra", "a", "R"], "ra,b": ["ra", "b", "R"], "ra,_": ["ca", "_", "L"],
  "rb,a": ["rb", "a", "R"], "rb,b": ["rb", "b", "R"], "rb,_": ["cb", "_", "L"],
  "ca,a": ["back", "_", "L"], "ca,b": ["no", "b", "S"], "ca,_": ["yes", "_", "S"],
  "cb,b": ["back", "_", "L"], "cb,a": ["no", "a", "S"], "cb,_": ["yes", "_", "S"],
  "back,a": ["back", "a", "L"], "back,b": ["back", "b", "L"], "back,_": ["s", "_", "R"],
} });
for (const w of ["abba", "aba", "abab", ""]) {
  const r = pal.run(w);
  PRINT(JSON.stringify(w), r.status, "in", r.steps, "steps");
}

// The same language by a grammar
const g = grammar("S -> a S a | b S b | a | b | ε");
["abba", "aba", "abab"].map((w) => g.accepts(w))
```
